{{Short description|Class of canonical diffraction integrals}}

[[File:Plot of absolute value of Pearcey integral.png|thumb|A plot of the absolute value of the Pearcey integral as a function of its two parameters.]]
[[File:A photograph of a cusp caustic.png|thumb|A photograph of a cusp caustic produced by illuminating a flat surface with a laser beam through a droplet of water.]]

In [[mathematics]], the '''Pearcey integral''' is defined as<ref>Frank W. J. Olver, Daniel W. Lozier, Ronald F. Boisvert, Charles W. Clark, NIST Handbook of Mathematical Functions, p.&nbsp;777, Cambridge, 2010</ref>

: <math>\operatorname{Pe}(x,y)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty \exp(i(t^4+xt^2+yt)) \, dt.</math>

The Pearcey integral is a class of canonical diffraction [[integrals]], often used in [[wave propagation]] and optical [[diffraction]] problems.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1017/CBO9780511753626|title=Hadamard Expansions and Hyperasymptotic Evaluation|year=2011|last1=Paris|first1=R. B.|isbn=9781107002586|url={{Google books|title=Hadamard Expansions and Hyperasymptotic Evaluation|8WggWK8AecIC|page=207|plainurl=yes}}}}</ref> The first numerical evaluation of this integral was performed by [[Trevor Pearcey]] using the quadrature formula.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1080/14786444608561335|title=XXXI. The structure of an electromagnetic field in the neighbourhood of a cusp of a caustic|year=1946|last1=Pearcey|first1=T.|journal=The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science|volume=37|issue=268|pages=311–317}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1090/mcom/3164 |title=Analytic formulas for the evaluation of the Pearcey integral |year=2016 |last1=López |first1=José L. |last2=Pagola |first2=Pedro J. |journal=[[Mathematics of Computation]] |volume=86 |issue=307 |pages=2399–2407|arxiv=1601.03615 }}</ref>
[[File:Circle caustic.png|thumb|Reflective caustic generated from a circle and parallel rays. On one side, each point is contained in three light rays; on the other side, each point is contained in one light ray.]]
In [[optics]], the Pearcey integral can be used to model diffraction effects at a [[Caustic (optics)|cusp caustic]], which corresponds to the boundary between two regions of geometric optics: on one side, each point is contained in three light rays; on the other side, each point is contained in one light ray.
